name: Turkesterone

lead: Turkesterone is a phytoecdysteroid, a plant steroid structurally related to insect molting hormones, first isolated from Ajuga turkestanica. It became popular in supplements as a purported natural anabolic.

Claims rest largely on rodent studies and on research into the better-known ecdysterone. Human trials of turkesterone specifically are small and mostly have not shown meaningful muscle or strength benefits; the wiki's rating is limited.

paras: In animals, ecdysteroids appear to increase muscle protein synthesis, possibly via estrogen receptor beta and signalling pathways, rather than through the androgen receptor. How well turkesterone is absorbed and whether these findings apply to people are unresolved.

It is sold as a dietary supplement in the US, with unresolved novel-food status in the EU. Short-term human studies have not reported serious harm, but long-term data are lacking, and independent testing has found products containing far less turkesterone than labelled.

lead: Turkesterone is a naturally occurring phytoecdysteroid, a plant steroid related to the molting hormones of insects, found in Ajuga turkestanica and several other plants, including Vitex species, Cyanotis arachnoidea, wheat and Rhaponticum acaule [1][2]. It is sold as a dietary supplement and promoted to bodybuilders as a natural anabolic, often described by sellers as an alternative to anabolic steroids [2][3].

Most of the supporting claims come from animal and cell research and from work on the related compound ecdysterone [2][4]. Wikipedia states that turkesterone is under laboratory research for anabolic effects through PI3K and AKT signalling and that its pharmacokinetics, bioavailability and effects in humans remain to be determined [1].

Human data specific to turkesterone are limited to small short-term studies. A 2024 preliminary study of acute doses in 11 men found no significant effects on IGF-1, resting metabolic rate or lipid and carbohydrate metabolism [5]. The compound is not an androgen in the usual sense; proponents describe an estrogen receptor beta-linked or non-androgenic route, a view that appears in forum discussion [3].
infobox: Ajuga turkestanica, Vitex spp., Cyanotis arachnoidea, Rhaponticum acaule [1]
Sold as a dietary supplement; not an approved drug

paras: Turkesterone is used by lifters in the hope of increased muscle growth, strength and recovery, and is sometimes added to cutting or 'natural' stacks and to TRT regimens. T Nation members describe trying it for experimentation, adding it to pre-workouts alongside laxogenin and ecdysterone, using it during a cut and taking it for its supposed effect on SHBG [6][7][8][9][10]. One forum poster says turkesterone has 'even more fakes' than a related supplement [3].

A 2024 review of ecdysterone and turkesterone describes their potential in sport and nutrition and in conditions such as chronic fatigue, cardiovascular and neurodegenerative disorders, largely on preclinical evidence [4].

A preliminary study of multiple acute turkesterone doses in 11 healthy men reported no significant main effects on serum IGF-1, resting metabolic rate or lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, although IGF-1 was numerically higher with turkesterone; the authors said the data do not fully support turkesterone as a potent anabolic supplement but are foundational for further work [5]. A review titled 'Phytoecdysteroids do not have anabolic effects in skeletal muscle' has also been published [11], and a trial of an ecdysteroid supplement examined physical and mental performance indices [12]. Grokipedia reports additional 2024 and 2025 randomised trials with no improvement in muscle growth or performance, a claim from an AI-generated source that was not independently verified [2].

Grokipedia says animal studies indicate low toxicity [2]. One T Nation poster reports that taking turkesterone at night raised blood pressure and heart rate somewhat and worsened sleep scores for them, so they moved to mornings [13]. Long-term human safety has not been established in the sources cited. Another forum poster describes concern about teenagers in a gym discussing SARMs, turkesterone, testosterone and trenbolone [14].

Turkesterone has a polyhydroxylated structure on a cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene skeleton similar to cholesterol-derived steroids [1]. Proposed anabolic action runs through PI3K and AKT signalling [1]; forum posts describe a pathway different from conventional steroids and claim it increases SHBG [3][9]. Pharmacokinetics, bioavailability and human effects are listed as undetermined by Wikipedia [1]. Related lab work includes studies of minor ecdysteroids from Ajuga turkestanica and 1970s Soviet experiments comparing turkesterone with the anabolic steroid nerobol in rat liver [15][16].

Ecdysone was found in silkworm pupae in 1954 by Adolf Butenandt and Peter Karlson, and turkesterone was first reported in 1973 from Ajuga turkestanica by a team in Tashkent, with its structure elucidated in 1975, according to Grokipedia [2]. A 1978 Soviet paper studied turkesterone and nerobol effects on mouse liver protein synthesis [16]. In forum culture, a 2021 thread notes that turkesterone was 'becoming very popular (again)', citing old mouse studies that reported it was more effective than Dianabol in mice [17].

Human studies of turkesterone itself are few: a 2024 preliminary investigation of multiple acute doses on IGF-1 and metabolic rate in 11 men [5], a trial of an ecdysteroid supplement on performance indices [12], and, according to Grokipedia, further 2024 to 2025 randomised trials [2]. Reviews of ecdysteroids in sport are available [4][11]. Animal work includes rodent studies of phytoecdysteroids as erythropoiesis stimulators and of Rhaponticum extracts on adipogenesis [18][19].
